procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court in Tamil Nadu since the High Court appeal concerns convictions under the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 05.08.2019 passed by the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court in Criminal Appeal (MD) No. 186 of 2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant filed Criminal Appeal (MD) No. 186 of 2019 in the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court. The High Court partly allowed the appeal by acquitting the Appellant under Section 309 IPC, but upheld the conviction under Section 302 IPC.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal by setting aside the order of the State of Tamil Nadu rejecting the Appellant's prayer for premature release.

directions: the order of the State of Tamil Nadu as contained in G.O. (D) No. 1127 dated 24.09.2019 issued by the Home (Prison-IV) Department, under the signature of Additional Chief Secretary to Government, rejecting the prayer for premature release of the Appellant, is set aside.
the Appellant is directed to be released forthwith, if not required in any other case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the State Government was justified in rejecting the appellant's prayer for premature release.

facts: The appellant was convicted for murdering her two children by administering poison and had served nearly 20 years in prison.
She applied for premature release, and a State Level Committee recommended her for it.
The State Government rejected this recommendation, arguing that the crime was cruel and brutal, and was committed so the appellant could continue an illicit relationship without hindrance.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the State's reasoning for rejecting the premature release.

The Court found that the appellant did not kill her children to continue her affair. Instead, she was under "tremendous mental stress" and acted out of "disappointment and frustration" after a quarrel with her paramour.
The Court noted that the appellant's act was an attempt to commit suicide along with her children, and she was only prevented from taking her own life by her niece.

Given these circumstances and the positive recommendation from the State Level Committee, the Court concluded that there was "no valid reason/justifiable ground" for the State to reject the recommendation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found that the State Government was not justified in rejecting the appellant's prayer for premature release. It set aside the State's rejection order and directed that the appellant be released.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the State Government was justified in rejecting the appellant's prayer for premature release.
appellant_arguments: The appellant pressed into service the cases of Guruswami Pillai v State, 1991 (1) MWN (Cr.) 153 and Suyambukkani v State, 1989 SCC OnLine Mad 481 to support the prayer for premature release.
respondent_arguments: The State argued that the premature release was rightly refused because the appellant's act of administering poison to young children and causing their death was cruel and brutal.
The State also submitted that the conviction under Section 302 of the IPC was upheld by the High Court after careful consideration of the merits.

cases.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v Rayavarapu Punnayya
cases.principle: Used as a legal benchmark ('on the anvil of') to test the facts of the case, against which the appellant's arguments were found not to be beneficial.

cases.case_name: State of Uttarakhand v Sachendra Singh Rawat
cases.principle: Factored into the court's reasoning and overall analysis of the case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The benefit of premature release for prisoners serving a life sentence is subject to the condition of completing a minimum of ten years of incarceration.
obiter: The precedents in Guruswami Pillai v State and Suyambukkani v State were determined by their own specific facts.
The ruling in State of Andhra Pradesh v Rayavarapu Punnayya does not benefit the appellant's position in this specific case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The State Government's rejection of the appellant's premature release was unjustified because it was based on an incorrect factual premise. The State claimed the appellant murdered her sons to continue an illicit relationship, but the Court found that, on the contrary, she had attempted to commit suicide along with her children out of disappointment and frustration following a quarrel with her paramour. This factual distinction undermined the State's entire rationale that the act was cruel and brutal in the manner it had described.
legal_tests_applied: The court assessed the State's decision against the established eligibility criteria for premature release for life convicts, which includes a minimum completion of ten years of incarceration as per G.O.(Ms) No. 64 dated 01.02.2018.

The court reviewed the executive decision of the State to ensure it was based on correct facts, especially when it contradicted a positive recommendation from the State Level Committee for premature release.
policy_considerations: This Court is not an institution to sermonise society on morality and ethics and we say no further on this score, bound as we are, by the brooding presence of the rule of law.
